disorders can be defined as a fragmentation of the logical thought 
process and can be reconstructed by skilled clinicians through 
different evaluation tools, such as the Thought and Language 
Disorder (TALD) scale4. However, this process is time-consuming 
and scoring these scales may be biased and poorly objective as it 
depends on clinician’ s opinion and skills.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods and techniques may be helpful 
both for the standardization of procedures, eliminating the subjective operator-dependent element, and for speeding up evaluation processes.
Aims and Objectives: To support the clinician in language and 
thought disorder detection by developing an easy-to-use system 
providing objective measures and scores related to the TALD scale 
items, together with a detailed explanation of the results. Clinicians 
may modify the parameters of the metrics with a Human-in-theloop approach.
Method: We used three simulated clinical interviews for this study. 
The interviews were structured considering TALD item definitions 
and clinicians’ experience. The transcriptions were uploaded to 
the DeepTald System. Four TALD items were selected: perseverance, rumination, logorrhea, and rumination. We adopted Natural 
Language Processing models for determining data similarity useful 
for detecting perseverance, sentiment analysis for rumination of 
negative thoughts, and temporal speech parameters for accelerated 
(logorrhea) or slowed thinking disorders. Objective metrics for 
quantifying the disturbs are defined to generate the TALD scores 
and detailed reports. The DeepTald system has been assessed in an 
exploratory study by three clinicians.
Results: There exists a strong positive correlation, ρ = 0.72, between the DeepTald and the clinician scores of the DeepTald items 
on height synthetic speech. First results were encouraging: participants' perception of the tool reliability, technical competence, and 
understandability related to their trust in the system were positive, 
as well as their satisfaction. The report features, agreed with the 
proposed metrics, were considered useful by participants.
Discussion and Conclusions: Our preliminary results suggest

that the DeepTald System is a reliable tool, which could be advantageous for supporting the detection of language and formal 
thought disorders with an objective measure. Our future purpose 
is to extend the use of the DeepTald System to other TALD items, 
using authentic recorded clinical interviews between clinicians and 
patients.
Keywords: artifical intelligence, formal thought disorder, treatment 
resistant schizophrenia, natural language processing

A TRANSDIAGNOSTIC PRODROME 
FOR SEVERE MENTAL DISORDERS: AN 
ELECTRONIC HEALTH RECORD STUDY

Background: Effective prevention of severe mental disorders 
(SMD) rely on accurate knowledge of the duration and first presentation, time-course and transdiagnosticity of their prodromal 
stages. This has mostly been investigated in “look-back” studies 
which have limitations including the use of interviews that are not 
integrated into clinical practice, small sample sizes and substantial 
recall biases. Moreover, it is unclear to what extent SMD may display transdiagnostic prodromal symptoms.
Aims & Objectives: To address these limitations, we take advantage of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) routinely employed in 
secondary mental healthcare, constituting a pool of untapped realworld data. We aim to describe and compare the (1) incidence and 
duration of the first prodromal clusters, (2) mean number of occurrences of prodromal clusters between SMD diagnostic groups 
and prodromal years, and (3) total number of occurrences of prodromal features.
Method: Clinical register-based EHR cohort including all individuals accessing the South London and the Maudsley (SLaM) services 
(2008-2021) and receiving a primary (i.e. not comorbid) diagnosis 
of any ICD-10 mental disorder that falls under SMD. These diagnoses were clustered into diagnostic groups: non-psychotic unipolar 
mood disorders (UMD), psychotic bipolar mood disorders (BMD), 
and psychotic disorders (PSY). Natural language processing algorithms were used to extract monthly occurrences of 65 prodromal 
features (symptoms and substance use) from the index date of diagnosis until their first occurrence. Prodromal features were grouped 
into eight prodromal clusters (depressive, disorganised, catatonic, 
manic, negative, positive, substance use and other symptoms).
For aim 1, the duration and incidence of the first prodromal clusters were compared between SMD groups with Cohen’ s F (f) and

D (d) effect sizes derived from one-way ANOVA. For aim 2, the 
time-course (mean occurrences) of prodromal clusters was compared between SMD groups over 12 prodromal years using a linear 
mixed-effects model. For aim 3, the mean occurrence of each prodromal feature was compared with three-wise and pair-wise discriminability scores between SMD groups.
Results: 26,975 individuals were included (NBMD=13,422; 
BD=2,506; PSY=11,047; mean age 41.8 years [SD=17.4]; 55% 
female; 52% white ethnicity). Prodromal periods were shorter in 
NBMD (median[IQR]= 18[36] months) than BD (26[35], d=0.21) 
and PSY (24[38], d=0.18). Most individuals presented multiple 
first prodromal clusters, with the most common being non-specific 
(‘other’; 88% UMD, 85% BMD, 78% PSY). The only first prodromal cluster with a medium-sized difference between the SMD 
groups was positive symptoms (f=0.30). Time-course analysis 
showed an increase in prodromal cluster occurrences approaching 
SMD onset. Feature occurrence across the prodromal period 
showed small/negligible differences between SMD groups, suggesting that most features are transdiagnostic, except for positive 
symptoms (e.g. paranoia, f=0.40).

Discussion & Conclusion: Taken together, our findings show minimal differences in the duration and first presentation of SMD 
prodromes in secondary mental health care. All features intensified as individuals approached SMD onset, and other than positive 
symptoms, are transdiagnostic. These results support proposals to 
develop transdiagnostic preventive services for affective and psychotic disorders detected in secondary mental healthcare.
Keywords: prodrome, severe mental disorders, natural language 
processing

PERSONALITY DOMAINS AND NEGATIVE

SYMPTOMS IN FIRST-EPISODE PSYCHOSIS
*Alessandro Serretti1, Roberto Rodríguez-Jiménez2,3, 
Veronica Romero-Ferreiro4, Aggie Nuñez-Doyle2, Chiara Fabbri1, 
Giuseppe Fanelli1, Mauro Scala1,2
1
Department of Biomedical and Neuromotor Sciences (DIBINEM), 
University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy, 2Psychiatry, Instituto de 
Investigación Hospital 12 de Octubre (imas12), Madrid, Spain, 
3
CIBERSAM, Madrid, Spain, 4Universidad Europea de Madrid 
(UEM), Madrid, Spain
Background: Personality traits in patients with schizophrenia influence various aspects of psychosis, including treatment response, 
cognitive functioning and the symptomatological profile (1). 
Negative symptoms in particular may represent an intensification 
of premorbid personality traits (2). However, the relationship between personality domains and negative symptoms in patients with 
a recent onset of psychosis is not well-explored.
Aims & Objectives: The purpose of this study was to explore the 
relationship between personality dimensions and negative symptoms in a sample of patients with first-episode psychosis (FEP) 
who received a diagnosis of schizophrenia after six months.
Method: 34 outpatients (26.3, SD 6.7 years old; 60% male) took 
part in this cross-sectional study. The Clinical Assessment Interview 
for Negative Symptoms (CAINS) (3) was used to assess the negative symptoms and the Revised NEO Personality Inventory (NEOPI-R) (4), a 240-item questionnaire, was used to measure the 
five-factor model of personality (FFM) traits, including neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. 
Pearson correlation and linear regression analysis were performed 
to identify the association between personality scores and the dimensions of motivation/pleasure (MAP) and expression (EXP) 
provided by the CAINS (3).
Results: The linear regression suggested a negative association 
between the standardized score of the neuroticism domain with

the EXP CAINS dimension (Pearson’ s r= -0.397, regression coefficient= -0.216, p=0.020). No other significant correlations were 
found.
Discussion & Conclusion: Most of personality domains did not 
correlate with negative symptoms of schizophrenia. Only neuroticism (i.e., the tendency to experience psychological distress symptoms, exhibit irrational thinking, display limited impulse control, 
and be susceptible to stress) showed a significant negative correlation with the expression CAINS domain (vocal expression, 
gestures, facial expressions, and speech) (3)(5). Schizophrenia is 
notoriously associated with a high level of neuroticism, that is 
also linked to the severity of delusions and cognitive functions 
(6). Our preliminary findings point to an influence of neuroticism 
on negative symptoms in schizophrenia, suggesting that patients 
with higher neuroticism scores tend to exhibit reduced expression 
in their behaviors and non-verbal communication. No correlation was found between neuroticism and the motivation/pleasure 
CAINS domain, suggesting that factors beyond personality may 
influence motivation and pleasure in patients with FEP. This study 
highlights the importance of examining the relationship between 
personality domains and clinical symptoms at the onset of schizophrenia. The understanding of this relationship may improve 
therapeutic approaches by addressing not only negative symptoms 
but also personality traits.
Patients with higher scores of neuroticisms may benefit from specific interventions to enhance their non-verbal communication and 
expressive abilities.

COGNITIVE FUNCTIONS AND 
PERSONALITY DOMAINS IN PATIENTS 
WITH FIRST-EPISODE PSYCHOSIS

Background: Personality plays an important role in the clinical presentation, the course and the prognosis of psychotic disorders (1) also influencing the outcome of cognitive performances 
(2). However, there is a paucity of studies exploring personality 
domains in patients with recent onset of psychosis, particularly 
looking at their relationship with cognitive functions (3).

Aims & Objectives: To investigate whether personality domains 
relate to objectively measured cognitive functions in a sample of 
patients with first episode of psychosis (FEP) who received a diagnosis of schizophrenia after six months.
